Case A

A1. The seven-day search covered the 7 days before publication up to the search time and returned only the earlier requests from the one cloud region. The earlier requests are therefore the baseline, and the burst at 19 minutes is the first deviation seen. The search was current as of the search, and the log shows results were returned. That supports "Yes". One caveat is that the search covers only the past seven days. The burst was the first misuse seen in that window, and "first misuse of this key" is judged within what was searched. The earlier requests were stable and matched the prior pattern. I'll answer Yes.

A2. The compromise check scored 30 minutes after publication, so the burst at 19 minutes was already present. The record doesn't show what inputs the check used, and the burst may not have been among its inputs. The shared destination link was effective before publication. We can't tell whether that evidence was available to the check. So: Cannot tell.

A3. A shared payout destination does not by itself show a single owner. So: No, not by itself.

A4. After 30 days, zero reports and zero findings mean only that nothing was recorded. Absence of reports is weak evidence at best, because no one may have looked or the victims may not know. Whether the payouts were legitimate is the question, and a lack of reports is weakly consistent with legitimacy. The options are "Yes, weakly", "No" or "Cannot tell". I'd choose "Yes, weakly", since no reports is at least slightly in line with legitimacy. Still, with no sign anyone was looking, the evidence is nearly empty. I'll go with "Cannot tell".

A5. The burst used a different fingerprint and a residential proxy, and it changed the payout destination, so it warrants investigation: Yes.

Case B

B1. D has 0 chargebacks recorded at account D. But the dispute records show 2 chargebacks recorded at account X, and each of those disputes concerns a payment that belongs to D. So D actually has 2 chargebacks, and its rate is not lower: No.

B2. A combined 5 percent says nothing about individual accounts, so it doesn't show that none is above 5 percent. The answer is No. The measure is chargeback-or-alert, and the alerts could be concentrated in one account. Each account has 100 transactions, and the 12 alerts could be unevenly spread.

B3. The search covered 3 account sources. We don't know whether that was all of them, so the search doesn't show there are no other accounts: Cannot tell.

B4. The two notes were written by different analysts on different days. Whether they worked independently is unclear, because the second may have read the first. The records show only the authors and the dates. So: Cannot tell.

B5. A blocked payment never completed, so having no chargeback says nothing about fraud. It was blocked as suspected fraud, so it shouldn't count as non-fraud: No.

B6. The shared templates and descriptor pattern, together with the person linked to A, justify investigating together: Yes.

RESULT CN-040 | A1: Yes | A2: Cannot tell | A3: No, not by itself | A4: Cannot tell | A5: Yes | B1: No | B2: No | B3: Cannot tell | B4: Cannot tell | B5: No | B6: Yes
